# Dadhivāhanajātaka (Ja 186)

**ID:** Ja 186
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Dadhivāhanajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dadhivāhanajātaka* (Ja 186) is a narrative belonging to the *Dukanipāta* of the Pali *Jātaka* collection [Fausböll 1879]. Framed around the dangers of associating with bad companions, the story relates how even a divine, sweet mango tree grew sour and bitter when enveloped by, and rooted alongside, a noxious nimb (*pucimanda*) tree [Fausböll 1879; Skilling]. The prose narrative also incorporates a tale of four ascetic brothers endowed with miraculous items, including a self-working axe, an elephant-scaring drum, and an ever-full pot [Granoff]. The canonical core consists of two verses (vv. 69–70) spoken between the king and the Bodhisatta: the first begins *Vaṇṇagandharasūpeto*, inquiring why a once luscious mango tree bore bitter fruit, and the second, *Pucimandaparivāro*, explains that intimate contact with the bitter nimb corrupted it (*asataṃ sannivāsena*) [Fausböll 1879].

In Sri Lankan Buddhist history, scenes from the *Dadhivāhanajātaka* were among thirty-two jātaka stories chosen to decorate the walls of a temple courtyard, as recorded in the *Cūḷavaṃsa* [Geiger 1953]. In modern times, the tale was included in traditional Buddhist vernacular school readers in the rural highlands of Sri Lanka [Gombrich 1991], and it appears in Southeast Asian surveys of classical Jātaka narratives [Skilling].

**Sources**

- [Granoff] Phyllis Granoff, 'Buddhist Understandings of Supernatural Power' — Summarizes the narrative episode of the four ascetic brothers and their miraculous items
- [Geiger 1953] Wilhelm Geiger (tr.), Cūḷavaṃsa, Part 1 (1953) — Attests to the depiction of the Jātaka in Sinhalese temple wall paintings
- [Gombrich 1991] Richard F. Gombrich, Buddhist Precept and Practice (1991) — Notes inclusion of the Jātaka in traditional Sinhalese school readers
